passage:
Saturday
Told Salma today. Properly. Not "sorry if you felt bad". I said, "I've been checking on you because I feel insecure, not because you did anything. That's my problem, and I'm going to stop."
She was quiet, then said, "Thank you. It's been hard." Her eyes were wet. I didn't realise how hard.
Rules for me, starting now: no asking who she was with. No reading her chats. When the tight feeling comes, I write it here instead of messaging her.
Also, on Thursday I went to Mr D'Souza, the school counsellor. It was awkward, but he didn't laugh. He said a boy admitting this takes guts, that controlling someone is a sign to get help, and he's seeing me every week for a while.
It's day one. I already wanted to check her status twice. I didn't.
Kiran

qa.q: Who is the school counsellor Kiran went to?
qa.a: Kiran went to Mr D'Souza, the school counsellor.

qa.q: How did Salma feel when Kiran told her the truth?
qa.a: Salma felt relieved and moved; her eyes were wet, and she said it had been hard. 🤍

qa.q: Which of Kiran's steps make real change likely?
qa.a: Kiran owned the insecurity, set clear rules against checking, writes feelings down instead, and is getting weekly help from the counsellor.

qa.q: What is day one of the new rules like for Kiran?
qa.a: It is hard for Kiran: he already wanted to check her status twice but didn't, and writes the tight feeling down instead of messaging her.

grounding: Shows a teen boy honestly telling his girlfriend the checking came from his insecurity, stopping it, and involving a school counsellor.

passage:
Jagdish waited for Radha by the banyan tree near the village school, where they always met on the way home. His cousin Kishore bhaiya had talked with him the night before, on the charpai under the stars, for a long time.

When Radha came, Jagdish didn't ask who she'd been talking to at the well. He'd asked that every day for a month.

Instead he said, "I need to tell you something. I've been checking on you because I felt I wasn't good enough for you. That was my problem, not yours. I'm sorry. I'm going to stop."

Radha looked at him carefully. "You'll stop asking who I talk to?"

"I'll stop. And if I can't, Kishore bhaiya says I should talk to Masterji about it. He's helped other boys."

Radha was quiet. Then she handed him half her roasted corn. "Okay. We'll see."

It wasn't forgiveness yet. But it was a start.

qa.q: Where did Jagdish and Radha always meet on the way home?
qa.a: By the banyan tree near the village school.

qa.q: How does Radha seem to feel when she says "Okay. We'll see"?
qa.a: She seems cautious and a little hopeful, willing to trust him again but waiting to see if he really stops.

qa.q: What makes Jagdish's step a healthy one?
qa.a: He tells Radha honestly about his insecurity, apologises, stops checking, and has a plan to talk to Masterji, an elder, if he can't stop.

qa.q: What might Jagdish be feeling as he waits for Radha's answer?
qa.a: He is probably nervous and ashamed, but also relieved to have said the truth.

grounding: Jagdish tells Radha honestly that he felt insecure and stops checking on her, with an elder to turn to if the pattern doesn't stop.

passage:
In Toronto, Ivan and Ana had been together since the autumn. By February, Ivan was checking her location three times a day and asking who she'd texted.

He had tried to stop. After a talk with his friend Siddiq, he'd even told Ana, "I get jealous because I feel I'm not enough." She'd been kind about it. He stopped for a week.

Then Ana went to a movie with her lab partner, and Ivan found himself outside the cinema, waiting. He didn't go in. He just waited.

When Ana saw him, her face went pale. "You followed me."

"I just wanted to see..."

That weekend they went together to the school counsellor, Ms Okafor, as Siddiq had urged. She listened to both of them. At the end Ana said quietly, "I don't feel safe like this."

Ivan nodded. He didn't argue. They ended it that afternoon, and Ms Okafor set up sessions for Ivan on his own.

qa.q: What did Ivan do when Ana went to a movie with her lab partner?
qa.a: He waited outside the cinema.

qa.q: What does Ana's face going pale show about how she feels?
qa.a: It shows she felt shocked and frightened, realising Ivan had followed her.

qa.q: Why was ending the relationship the healthier choice here?
qa.a: Ivan's checking kept coming back even after he tried to stop, so it wasn't safe for Ana; involving the counsellor gave both support and gave Ivan help of his own.

qa.q: How might Siddiq see the outcome?
qa.a: He may feel sad for his friend but relieved that Ivan is finally getting real help from the counsellor.

grounding: When Ivan's controlling pattern returns despite honesty, he and Ana accept the relationship is not healthy and involve the school counsellor.

The counsellor's room at the school in Jaipur had a small window and a box of tissues on the table. Ritu had come alone.

"Nishant said sorry last month," she told Devika ma'am. "He said he was jealous because he felt insecure. He promised to stop checking my phone."

"And did he?"

"For two weeks. Then yesterday he took my phone out of my bag while I was in the washroom. He read my chats with my cousin."

Devika ma'am listened without interrupting. "How do you feel now?"

"Scared. And tired. I don't want to be watched all the time."

"What do you want to do?"

Ritu took a breath. "End it."

"That's a sound choice. I'd like to call your mother today so she knows, and I'll speak to Nishant with his class teacher. You don't have to handle him alone."

Ritu nodded. For the first time in weeks, she felt a little lighter.

qa.q: What did Nishant do while Ritu was in the washroom?
qa.a: He took her phone out of her bag and read her chats with her cousin.

qa.q: How does Ritu feel before and after her talk with Devika ma'am?
qa.a: Before, she feels scared and tired of being watched; afterwards, she feels a little lighter.

qa.q: How does Devika ma'am respond, and why is it wise?
qa.a: She listens, supports Ritu's choice to end it, calls her mother the same day, and arranges to speak to Nishant with his class teacher, so Ritu isn't alone.

qa.q: What might Nishant experience when the counsellor and teacher speak to him?
qa.a: He may feel ashamed or defensive, but it gives him a chance to face the controlling pattern with adult help.

grounding: When Nishant's controlling checking returns after his apology, Ritu chooses to end it with a counsellor's support, which involves her mother and his teacher.

Dear Rekha Ma'am,
Thank you for seeing me on Monday. I wanted to tell you what happened after.
I spoke to Faraz on Tuesday, the way we practised. He was honest too. He said he feels insecure when I'm with my debate team, and he promised to stop asking for my phone. For three days he did. On Saturday he asked for my location "just once", then again at nine, then at ten.
On Sunday we talked again, calmly, at the park near my house. He said, "I don't think I can stop right now." I said, "Then this isn't good for either of us." We both cried a bit. We agreed to end it.
I told Ammi that night, and she sat with me for a long time.
Could I come and see you again this week? I think I need to understand why I kept apologising.
Noor

qa.a: They talked again, calmly, on Sunday at the park near Noor's house.

qa.q: How can you tell that Noor felt sad but sure about ending it?

qa.a: Noor spoke honestly with Faraz, gave his promise a real chance, ended it calmly when the checking returned, told Ammi that night and is going back to the counsellor.

qa.q: What is Faraz likely experiencing when he says, 'I don't think I can stop right now'?
qa.a: Faraz seems honest but ashamed and sad, recognising that his insecurity is stronger than his promise and that things cannot stay healthy like this.

grounding: Shows a teen giving an insecure partner's promise to stop checking a fair chance and, when the pattern returns, both accepting it is unhealthy, with a counsellor and parent involved.
